props.title: Yakuza: Like a Dragon
props.initialSlug: Yakuza soldier seeks revenge in brutal gang war

sections.content: Yakuza: Like a Dragon, directed by Takashi Miike, brings Sega's hit video game series to explosive life. This film adaptation captures the essence of Kamurocho's criminal underworld while delivering Miike's signature blend of ultra-violence and dark humor. Unlike failed game adaptations like Super Mario Bros. (1993) or Street Fighter (1994), Miike treats the source material with respect, maintaining the games' complex honor codes and brotherhood themes. The film follows Kazuma Kiryu's release from prison and subsequent entanglement in a massive conspiracy, much like Oldboy (2003) but with distinctly Japanese yakuza sensibilities.

sections.content: Miike's extensive yakuza filmography, including Dead or Alive (1999) and Ichi the Killer (2001), prepared him perfectly for adapting Like a Dragon. His understanding of both yakuza film traditions and video game aesthetics creates a unique hybrid that satisfies both audiences. The film's stylized violence echoes classics like Tokyo Drifter (1966) while incorporating the game's over-the-top heat actions and dramatic confrontations.

The film's success opened doors for better game adaptations in Japan, influencing works like Ace Attorney (2012) and Yakuza: Like a Dragon. Miike's approach demonstrates how to translate interactive storytelling to cinema without losing the core appeal that made the source material compelling. The film maintains the games' complex mix of serious crime drama and absurdist side stories that defined the series. SUBHEAD: Modern Yakuza Cinema Evolution

sections.content: Like a Dragon represents a crucial evolution in yakuza cinema, bridging traditional films like Battles Without Honor and Humanity (1973) with contemporary interpretations. Modern yakuza films increasingly reflect Japan's changing criminal landscape, as seen in Beyond Outrage (2012) and The Blood of Wolves (2018). These films maintain the genre's core themes while acknowledging how technology and globalization have transformed organized crime.
